opener.heading: Week 37: Backyard Explorers 🔍
about: Azlyn goes out with something to carry and comes back with something in it, seven days running. A six-cup box on Friday, a dishpan of soil with six things buried in it on Saturday, ten taped objects hidden round the yard on Sunday, a rucksack that empties one stop at a time on Wednesday. The finds table by the window goes up on Friday and stays up until Thursday, so everything she brings home has somewhere to live and something to sit beside.

Joseph's birthday lands on the Monday and that day belongs to him: sock beanbags and three buckets in the morning, a cardboard card the height of the front door in the afternoon, and her behind it at six o'clock. The rest of the week runs on soil, water, chalk and whatever the hedge is holding.
azlyn: Sorting to a rule. Something rough, something yellow, something with a hole in it. She holds the rule in her head while her hands do the searching.
Three ways to throw (roll, underarm, overarm), one bucket at each distance, so she can feel which pattern her body has today.
Counting down from ten. The rucksack empties one stop at a time and she says how many are left before you do.
Balance with her hands full. A low wall, then a route across the yard with a cup she has to keep under the line.
Two people, one job. A bucket slung on a broom handle goes nowhere until both ends move together.
you: Recovery isn't a switch, and pushing it backfires
Summer's best days are usually the least planned
Losing is a skill that isn't ready yet, and designing around that is not coddling
Throwing develops in a predictable order, and rushing it doesn't help
Balance comes from being slightly off it
Subtraction makes sense long before the symbols do
Cooperation is harder than competition, and it needs the same practice
shopping: A cereal box, for the finds cards
One large cardboard box, big enough to flatten and fold like a card
Bright masking tape or electrical tape, 1 roll
A stapler (adult only), or tape and glue
Washable poster paint and a wide brush, if the card gets painted
Old socks you don't want back, 3
Ten objects from round the house, none of them small enough to fit through a toilet-roll tube, to tape and hide
Six small objects to bury: a teaspoon, a jar lid, a clothespin, a pebble, a toy animal, an old key
Six things for the explorer bag: a spoon, a cup, a flashlight, a hat, a notebook, a hairbrush
About twenty odds and ends heaped up for Wednesday's packing
An apple, crackers and a small bottle of water for the rucksack
A bandage, a cloth and a small toy
A metal spoon and a teaspoon, plus old pans and spoons for the mud
A kitchen timer, or the one on your phone
A tote bag or small rucksack
A magnifying glass, if you have one
Old towels, 3, one of them large
Old clothes and a change of clothes, for both soil days
A heavy plant pot, or a bag of soil
Plant pots, or large tins and yogurt tubs with holes in the bottom, 3
A bag of soil or spare potting soil for Saturday's dig, enough to fill a dishpan
A trowel, or a big serving spoon
A handful of stones or gravel
Macadamia butter, or macadamias to blend into some
Children's antihistamine, if there is none in the house
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 15 months this week. He runs, spoons his own food, and points at pictures in books, and it is the same finger he aims at a spider web on the fence and at the same dog eleven times in the library.

days.title: The Explorer's Kit
days.prepTonight: Rinse an egg box and stand it upside down to dry, cut six cards out of a cereal box, and leave both on the table with the marker, the crayons and the masking tape.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Finds Table by the Window

opening.title: What an Explorer Carries
opening.need: 1 tote bag or small rucksack · 6 candidate items from round the house (a spoon, a cup, a flashlight, a hat, a notebook, a hairbrush) · 1 sheet of paper · 1 crayon.
steps: Lay the six candidates in a row and name each one out loud with her.
She picks four for the bag and the other two go back in the drawer. Take her choices as they come, hairbrush included.
Draw round each chosen thing on the paper, a list she can read without opening the bag. Tell her it needs one more thing, made at quarter past nine.

main.title: The Six-Cup Finds Box
materials: 1 length of string, about 3 feet, for a handle
steps: Cut the lid off and trim the base down to six cups. You cut, she holds the box still from the far side of the table.
Hand her the crayons. The outside is hers, every panel of it.

Draw one rule beside each cup with the marker, saying each out loud: something rough, something yellow, something with a hole in it, something smaller than her thumb, something that grew, something she has never seen before.
Pierce a hole either side with the scissor point, thread the string through and knot both ends so the box hangs at her hip.
Tape every torn corner. The box has to survive a hedge.
Run it once round the kitchen and fill one cup before you leave.
main.tip: Draw the rules, do not write them. She reads pictures, and the box works in her hands ten steps ahead of you.

outside.title: One Thing for Every Cup
paras: The hedge on your usual route is heavy with fruit and strung with old webs, and nothing has come off the trees yet. Walk that route with the morning's finds box on her hip and six jobs instead of one. Rough is easy, yellow is easy, and something with a hole in it will take her the longest. Six cups is the quota, so the seventh good stone stays where it is.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and runs. Give him a paper bag of his own and let him drop things in it at his own pace. He points at what he wants now, so name whatever he aims at, even a drain.

second.title: The Finds Table by the Window
second.intro: The six things come out of the box and get somewhere to live. The table stays up all week.
materials: The finds box and the six finds in it
1 tray, or a small side table by the window
1 old dish towel to lay it on
6 cards cut from a cereal box (cut last night)
1 saucer for the smallest things, to live on a shelf above Kreston's reach
The fruit bowl, to move off the table
steps: Spread the dish towel over the cleared tray or side table.
Unload the box one cup at a time. She decides where each find sits and you leave the arrangement alone.
Anything that rolls, or that would fit in Kreston's mouth, goes on the saucer, and the saucer sits on a shelf above the table. It comes down whenever she asks for it.
Hold up each find and ask what its card should say. Write her exact words with the marker, wrong grammar and all.
Prop each card in front of its find.
Leave a bare stretch at one end. Tell her that end is for tomorrow.
Walk Joseph past it when he gets in and stand back while she does the talking.
second.tip: A table that gets tidied on Sunday stops being hers. Give up the surface for the week and move the fruit bowl.

alternatives: Six finds straight onto the windowsill, the small ones on the high saucer, no cards and no table.
Sort the finds by color, then by size, then by which she would keep.
Draw all six on one big sheet instead of writing labels.
Wash the muddy ones in a bowl on the step and dry them on the towel.
outAgain: A café, cake and a window seat, and the finds box comes along on her shoulder
A friend's house, if anyone wants a visitor on a Friday
The playground, ten minutes only, so the morning's walk gets the credit
The corner store for something for the weekend, and let her carry it
Back out to the same hedge, to see what she walked past this morning

aroundWorld.title: Australia: Bush Tucker 🔍
paras: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families have gathered food from the Australian bush for tens of thousands of years, and the list is long: wattleseed, warrigal greens, quandong, finger lime, and the Kakadu plum, which carries more vitamin C than any other fruit anyone has measured. One bush food traveled the world and ended up in supermarkets everywhere. The macadamia is the only Australian native plant grown as a major food crop anywhere on earth.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Spread macadamia butter on toast for the snack, or blend a handful of macadamias to a paste yourself and let her push the button. Whole nuts stay out of reach of both of them.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Aboriginal groups managed macadamia trees for food long before anyone in Europe had seen one.

days.krestonPM: At 15 months he is at his best in a café for about half an hour. Sit him where he can watch the counter, order him something he can hold, and let him spoon it himself. He points at people now, so say out loud whatever he aims at.

insight.headline: Recovery isn't a switch, and pushing it backfires.
paras: Azlyn comes off a cold, or a run of loud days, looking mended by mid-morning and then falls apart at four over a sock. Energy returns before the reserve underneath it does, and the reserve is what she spends on holding herself together. Doctors expect a shorter fuse and heavier sleep for days after a fever has gone. A table by the window she can walk up to and walk away from asks nothing of her, and it will hold her longer today than a planned hour would. Leaving the plan half done costs you nothing. It shortens the tail.

days.safety: Kreston is 15 months, runs, and mouths what he picks up. The house fills with small found objects today. The table stays at her height, because a table she cannot get to is no use to her, and everything on it small enough to swallow goes on the saucer instead. The saucer lives on a shelf above his reach and comes down whenever she asks. The box comes off her shoulder at the front door. Nothing collected gets eaten. Unknown berries and mushrooms stay outside and stay unpicked, which matters more today because the sidebar is about wild food. September sun still catches fair skin on a whole morning out: hat on, cream before the door opens. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Dig
days.prepTonight: Fill a dishpan with soil and bury six objects in it after she is asleep, then put the sieve, the spoon, the old toothbrush and old clothes by the back door.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Afternoon With No Plan In It

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Finds Laid Out on Newspaper

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Bath That Takes Two Washes

opening.title: Spoon, Sieve, Toothbrush
opening.need: 1 metal spoon · 1 old toothbrush · 1 kitchen sieve or colander · 1 tray · 1 cup of dry soil.
steps: Line the three tools up on the tray and give each one its job: the spoon lifts, the sieve catches, the brush uncovers.
Tip the cup of dry soil onto the tray. She scoops with the spoon, shakes it through the sieve, and brushes the last off her palm.
Tell her something is buried in the dishpan outside and these three tools are how it comes out. Do not tell her how many.

main.title: What the Soil Was Hiding
materials: 1 dishpan of soil, or a patch of border
6 objects buried last night: a teaspoon, a jar lid, a clothespin, a pebble, a toy animal, an old key
steps: Old clothes on before the door opens. Set the dishpan of soil you buried the objects in last night on the ground, and stand the tray on the back step or a chair beside it, above Kreston's reach.
She digs with the spoon and every spoonful goes through the sieve, held over the tray.
Anything the sieve catches gets the toothbrush before it goes on the tray.
Rinse the caked ones in the pitcher and let her decide which need it.
Lay the finds out in the order she pulled them up, then count them together. Six.
If she wants them buried again, bury them again while she turns round.
main.tip: Say nothing about six until she has four. A child who knows the total digs to the number and stops.

outside.title: The Windfall Apples
paras: Mid-September and the apples are coming down on their own. Walk to whatever tree you know, a community garden fence or the one at the park, and pick up what is on the grass. Two piles: sound ones for the bowl, wasp-holed ones for the birds. She will want all of them, so agree a number before the bag comes out.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and spoons his own food now, the same wrist he needs here. Give him a bowl of water, a spoon and an empty tub of his own, well away from the soil. He will pour between them for a long stretch, and every miss teaches him where his hand ends up.

second.title: The Afternoon With No Plan In It
second.intro: You set it out and then you stop. Ninety minutes, one bucket of water, the soil she dug, and no instruction from you.
materials: The dug soil, still in its dishpan
A chair and a drink for you
steps: Spread the old sheet on the ground and stand the dishpan of soil in the middle.
Set the bucket at one end and heap the pans, spoons and pitcher beside it. Say nothing about what it is for.

Settle Kreston first. Indoors with another adult, or out on the sheet beside you with a hand's depth of water in his own bowl and the bucket within your arm's reach. The hands-off part of this afternoon is for Azlyn and never for him.
Take a drink outside and sit down where she can see you. When she asks what to do, tell her you do not know, and mean it.
Answer what she asks and nothing else. If she brings you a pan of mud, take the pan.
Top up the bucket when it empties. Tidy nothing, and let the sheet get destroyed.
At quarter past two, one towel for her and one for the floor, then the change of clothes at the back door.
second.tip: The first ten minutes look like failure. She will drift, ask twice more what she is supposed to do, and then start. Hold your nerve and the other eighty run themselves.

alternatives: The bucket and the pans on the step, and leave the soil out of it.
Wash every dug object in warm soapy water and line them up to dry.
Bury six new things for Joseph to find when he gets home.
Take the sheet and the pans indoors and do the whole thing with dry rice.
outAgain: The botanical garden, for the greenhouse and the long paths she can run
The park with the biggest trees you know, for buckeyes and acorns
A garden nursery, to look rather than buy
The riverside path, and count how many trees have turned
Home, hose, and nothing at all, if the morning was enough
days.krestonPM: He walks the greenhouse rather than rides it, and at 15 months that takes three times as long as carrying him. Let it. Everything in there is at his eye level and he stops at each one. Keep his hands off the leaves, which are not for chewing, and steer him with a hand on his back.

insight.headline: Summer's best days are usually the least planned.
paras: Watch what happens to her play when you stop supplying the next idea. The episodes get longer, the story gets more complicated, and she starts combining things you set out for separate purposes. Researchers who time children's play find that adult direction shortens episodes and narrows them, while the same child left with open materials stays with one thread far longer than a directed child does. Twenty minutes at three is a good run, and she comes back to it twice. Your ninety minutes today are the cheapest thing in the book and they will produce more than the morning did. Sitting there with a drink while she works is the whole job, and it counts as the plan.

days.safety: Garden soil carries cat and fox mess. Hands washed before anything goes near a mouth, and any cut on her hands covered before she starts digging. The six buried objects are all small enough for Kreston to choke on, and he is out in the yard with you for the whole dig. The tray stands on the step or a chair above his reach, every find goes onto it the moment the toothbrush is done with it, and all six get counted back onto it before anybody moves position. Give him a hand's depth of water in his bowl and no more, and tip it out on the grass when he loses interest. This afternoon you stop instructing Azlyn and you do not stop watching him: he stays within arm's reach for every minute the bucket holds water, and the bucket never gets left standing once you go in. Windfall apples this far into September have wasps working the holed ones, and a wasp in an apple stings the hand that closes on it. You turn every apple over before she picks it up, and the holed ones go straight on the pile for the birds. Mid-September sun still catches fair skin on a whole morning out: hat on, cream before the door opens.

days.title: Everybody Wins Something
days.prepTonight: Collect ten objects into a bag, every one of them too big to fit through a toilet-roll tube, and stand it by the door with the bright tape, the chalk, the timer and two buckets.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: A Strip of Tape on Everything

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Books in the Bottom of the Closet

opening.title: A Strip of Tape on Everything
opening.need: 10 objects from round the house, every one of them too big to fit through a toilet-roll tube · 1 roll bright masking tape or electrical tape · 1 bag.
steps: Tip the ten out of the bag you filled last night onto the table and count them out loud, sliding each one across as you say its number.
She tears a strip of tape for each and sticks it on so a flash of color shows from any angle. Crooked is fine and crooked is easier to spot.
Count them back into the bag, ten out and ten in, then send her upstairs while you hide them.

main.title: The Hunt Against the Timer
materials: 1 roll bright masking tape or electrical tape
1 kitchen timer, or a phone timer
steps: Stick a strip of tape on the back step. That is base. Nothing counts until it comes back to base.
Hide the ten while she waits inside. Half of them in plain sight, and the two biggest of the lot, a shoe and a wooden spoon, low enough for Kreston to reach on his own.
Give her one bucket and take the other. Three minutes on the timer, everybody hunting on the same side.
Chalk a mark on the path at base for every one that comes in, so the score is a row she can see instead of a number she has to hold.
If the timer goes with two still out, put another minute on rather than calling it finished.
Swap. She hides them, she sets the timer, and she gets to stand over you telling you how long is left.
main.tip: The timer is the opponent. Nobody is racing anybody in this house, and the beep is what everyone is up against.

outside.title: The Seeds That Spin Down
paras: Maples are dropping their helicopters now, and the tulip trees have their winged seeds down. Gather a pocketful, find the highest safe place to let go from, a step, the bottom of the slide, your shoulders, and drop them one at a time. Try one with a wing torn off. Try two stuck together. She will work out that the wing is doing something long before she can tell you what.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months, runs, and finding a bright taped thing on the grass is a whole game to him on its own. Point at the two low ones and let him get there first. He can carry one object while running now, which is newer than it looks, and he will bring it to you unasked.

second.title: Three Piles, One Each
second.intro: Ten things and three people. She does the dividing, all of it, and the last one is the interesting one.
steps: Write the three names on the three cards with the marker: Azlyn, Kreston, Brooklyn. Ask her afterwards which is which.
Space the cards along the tray and tip the haul into the middle.
She deals. One for me, one for Kreston, one for you, round and round, and your hands stay off the pile.
Ten will not go into three. Let her arrive at that herself, then let her decide what happens to the last one. Take her answer whatever it is.
Tape or glue each pile down onto its card once she says she is happy.
Ask her which of the three she would rather have. She will say her own, every time, and that is the right answer to a question about fairness at three.
Stand the three cards at the empty end of the finds table from Friday.
second.tip: The piles will not come out equal and you are not to fix them. Kreston's pile getting the broken one is a decision she made about who can be trusted with things.

alternatives: One pile each, straight into three pockets, and no cards.
Sort the haul by which things came from indoors and which did not.
Hide the ten again for the whole afternoon and hunt them one at a time.
Draw round all ten on one sheet and see whose shapes she can name.
outAgain: The long walk with the stroller, the full loop, no destination and no hurry
Feeding the ducks, and count the helicopters on the way
The playground on the far side, the one you have to walk to
A scooter run along the flat bit, with her helmet
The woods, where the leaves are starting to gather along the path edges
days.krestonPM: He gets his pile and he will take it apart inside a minute, which is a fair use of it. At 15 months he walks a good stretch of the loop before he wants the stroller, so start him on his feet and load him in when he slows. The helicopters stay in your pocket, and you drop one for him to watch spin on the way home.

insight.headline: Losing is a skill that isn't ready yet, and designing around that is not coddling.
paras: At three, Azlyn cannot yet hold "I lost the game" apart from "I am worse than you". The two arrive as one feeling, which is why a lost race produces a whole-body collapse rather than a shrug. Separating the outcome from the self is a piece of cognitive machinery that gets built between four and six, so a losing game this month costs you an afternoon and buys her nothing she can use yet. A shared timer gives her the same racing heart with nobody on the wrong end of it. You are matching the game to the equipment she has, and in two years you can hand her a game with a loser in it.

days.safety: Nothing that fits through a toilet-roll tube goes in the ten. Kreston is 15 months, runs, and mouths what he picks up, and he is out there with you for the whole hunt, so the two you leave low for him are the two biggest things in the bag. Count the ten out before you hide them and count the ten back into the bag at the end of every round, ten and ten, before anybody goes indoors. Bright tape lifts off in a wet hand, so check each strip as the objects come in and press the loose ones down again. His three glued things come apart inside a minute this afternoon, so stay with him while he has them and pick the pieces up off the floor when he is finished.

days.title: Dad's Birthday Games
days.prepTonight: Put three old socks, the rice, the rubber bands and the chalk by the back door, and hide the big flattened box behind the sofa.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Bucket She Can't Reach Yet

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Longest Throw on the Dry Grass

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Card as Big as the Door

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Candles and Dad's Place at the Table

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Waiting at the Window for Dad

opening.title: Filling the Sock Balls
opening.need: 3 old socks · 2 cups dry rice or lentils · 1 cup for scooping · rubber bands or string.
steps: Hold a sock open while she scoops the rice in a cup at a time. Fill each one to about a fist. Whatever lands on the floor stays there until all three are tied.
Twist the top, fold the cuff back down over the ball, and wind a rubber band round it twice. Three socks, three balls.
Let her drop each one on the tiles. They land dead and go nowhere. Say happy birthday to Dad while you work.

main.title: The Bucket She Can't Reach Yet
steps: Chalk a line across the path. Both feet stay behind it for every throw.
Bucket one, two steps out. She rolls the beanbags into it underarm along the ground. Three rolls, fetch, again.
Bucket two, five steps out. Underarm toss, palm up, let go at the top of the swing. Show her once, then leave her alone with it.
Bucket three, as far down the yard as you can put it and still see it. Overarm, and she will not reach it today.
Chalk a cross where each of her long throws lands. By the tenth the crosses have crept forward.
Put her name and the date beside the furthest cross. Bucket three stays out there all week.
main.tip: Do not walk bucket three in to make her day. She knows how far it is, and a bucket you moved is worth nothing to her by dinner.

outside.title: The Longest Throw on the Dry Grass
paras: The grass is still burnt yellow from August, hard enough for a beanbag to skid. Take all three to the green. Everyone throws in turn, and each longest throw gets marked with somebody's shoe until the next one beats it. Walk back and pace out the distance, with her counting the steps.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and throws by letting go, straight down, with no aim in it. Give him a beanbag and a bucket at his own feet so he gets the drop and the thud without needing distance. He will fill it, tip it out and fill it again.

second.title: The Card as Big as the Door
second.intro: One flattened box, one birthday, and a card Joseph has to walk into. She covers all of it herself.
materials: Crayons, or washable paint and a wide brush
steps: Flatten the box on the floor and fold it once down the middle so it opens like a card.
She covers the front, edge to edge. Crayons if you want the afternoon calm, paint if you have the patience for it. Your hands stay off.
Ask her what it should say. Write her words across the top with the marker, big, and let her make her own mark underneath as the signature.
Inside is Joseph. She draws him, and she adds whatever she says he likes. Ask, do not suggest.
Tape a length of string across the back as the hanger, three good strips at each end.
Hang it on the inside of the front door at his eye level, the first thing he meets tonight.
She stands behind the door, you open it, and she shouts. Run it twice so six o'clock has a shape she knows.
second.tip: Take a photo of the card flat on the floor before it goes on the door. She will want it in December.

alternatives: One sheet of paper, folded once, and the whole thing done in twenty minutes.
A birthday banner of taped-together cereal boxes instead of a card.
Draw round her hand five times and turn each one into something for Joseph.
Wrap three things from the house in newspaper and let him unwrap his own belongings.
outAgain: The playground with the big slide, and let her do it twelve times
The riverside path, if the playground is full of school pickup
The green space with a ball, to burn what the throwing did not
The corner store, and she chooses what goes with the candles
Straight home, if the card needs another half hour
days.krestonPM: At 15 months he can climb the low steps of the playground on his own, and he wants to. Stay a hand behind him and let him take them rather than lifting him up. The big slide is not his yet. He goes down the short toddler slide on his own, sitting up and feet first, with you standing at the bottom, because a shoe that catches on the way down twists the leg and an adult's weight behind it breaks the bone.

insight.headline: Throwing develops in a predictable order, and rushing it doesn't help.
paras: The order runs roll, underarm toss, then overarm, and it takes years rather than weeks. At three Azlyn throws with her arm alone: feet planted, shoulders square, no step and no twist through the trunk. The stepping, rotating throw most adults picture turns up between five and six, and no amount of correcting her elbow this morning brings it forward. Three buckets at three distances let her pick the pattern her body can do today and give her one it cannot, which is what keeps her coming back to the far one all week. Bucket three is the one she will tell Joseph about at six o'clock.

days.safety: Loose rice and lentils are the size Kreston chokes on at 15 months, so the socks get filled with him in the highchair and the floor gets swept before he is down on it. Nothing harder than a rice-filled sock gets thrown, and nothing gets thrown indoors. Keep the ground behind and in front of the throwing line clear. Kreston is 15 months and runs straight into things, so he stays behind the throwers or in the stroller, never between the line and the buckets. Mid-September sun still catches fair skin on a whole morning out on open grass: hat on, cream before the door opens. Candles at dinner get lit and blown out with both children sitting down, and the matches go straight back on a high shelf.

days.title: The Water Run
days.prepTonight: Stand three plastic cups, the marker, the chalk, a pitcher and two buckets by the back door, and pack the swim bag tonight.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Along the Top of the Low Wall

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Pouring the Drinks to the Line

opening.title: The Line Inside the Cup
opening.need: 3 plastic cups · 1 permanent marker · 1 pitcher of water · 1 old towel.
steps: Draw a line round the inside of each cup, a thumb's width down from the rim. She does one of the three, and hers will wander.
Spread the towel and let her pour from the pitcher up to the line in each cup. Let the first one overflow.
Carry a filled cup from the table to the back door and back, two hands, watching the water rather than her feet.

main.title: The Cup That Mustn't Spill
materials: 2 buckets, one at each end of the route
steps: Chalk a start and a finish across the yard and stand a bucket at each end. Fill the start bucket from the pitcher.
She dips a cup to its line, walks the route, and tips it into the finish bucket. No timing, no comment.
Walk it again fast. Chalk a cross on the ground wherever water lands, and the crosses stay all week.
Walk it slow, counting her steps out loud from start to finish.
Chalk a wavy line between the two buckets and send her along that instead of straight across.
Draw a second, lower line on one cup with the marker. She runs the whole route with that one and works out the trade between load and speed.
main.tip: Keep the old towel at the finish bucket and dry her hands between runs. Wet hands on smooth plastic account for most of the spilling, and she will blame her feet.

outside.title: Along the Top of the Low Wall
paras: Find the longest low wall on your route, the garden ones at knee height, and walk her along the top with one hand out and not holding her. September light comes in sideways and the wall is warm from yesterday. Go along, turn round, come back. Then have her carry something small in one hand and see how much harder the same wall gets.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and walking while carrying is his current project. Give him his own cup and his own bucket at the near end and let him make the trip in whatever direction he fancies. He will pour it down his front, which is how he learns where the rim is.

second.title: Following the Ant Road
second.intro: Down on the ground, knees on a folded towel, for something smaller than her thumbnail. Ninety minutes is the outside limit and thirty is a good afternoon, so let her come and go from the chalk marks as often as she likes. A cookie crumb starts it.
materials: 1 old towel, folded, to kneel on
A magnifying glass if you have one, or your phone camera zoomed in if you do not
steps: Find the crack in the path or the base of the wall where ants go in and out. Sit down on the ground with her.
Put the crumb down a hand's length from the crack and wait. Nothing happens for a few minutes.
Chalk a small mark wherever you both see an ant, so their road draws itself across the path.
Lay the craft stick flat across the line. Some ants go over, some go round, and the road bends within a minute.
Look at one through the magnifying glass, or zoom your phone camera in and hold the screen where she can see. Count the legs together.
She draws the road on the paper with the crayon: the crack, the crumb, the chalk marks, the stick across it.
Lift the stick and what is left of the crumb when you finish, and leave the chalk marks for the rain.
second.tip: Do not give the ants names or jobs. She will do that herself within ten minutes.

alternatives: One crumb, one chalk line, twenty minutes, and inside for a story.
Follow a woodlouse under a flowerpot instead.
Chalk the whole path into a map and drive cars round it.
Draw round her shadow at one o'clock and again at two.
outAgain: Swimming, and the water is warmer than the air by now
The splash pad, if the session is booked out
Indoor playground, on a Tuesday when it is empty
A short walk and an early bath, if the pool is too much today
The kiddie pool at home with the three cups from this morning
days.krestonPM: He swims too. At 15 months he walks down the shallow steps holding the rail with you a step below him, worth the extra five minutes. Hold him under the arms and let him kick across to the side. Out and dressed before he is cold, which comes on faster in September than August.

insight.headline: Balance comes from being slightly off it.
paras: Standing still on a flat floor teaches Azlyn nothing about balance. The system that keeps her upright learns from small losses and the corrections that follow, so the useful work happens on the wall top, on the curb, and on the wobbly walk across the yard with a cup she does not want to spill. Carrying something shifts where her weight sits and forces her to solve it again. Every time you let her walk the wall instead of lifting her over it, she banks another few hundred corrections, and the falls she does not take at six are paid for now.

days.safety: Two open buckets stand on the ground for an hour this morning. Empty both the moment the running stops, and never leave one standing while you are indoors. Kreston gets a hand's depth in his own bucket and no more, and he stays within arm's reach of you for every minute any of the three holds water. At the pool both of them stay within arm's reach of you, from the changing room door until you are back through it. September wasps go for anything sweet and they sting without much provocation. The bait stays a dry crumb, no sugar water, and no open cups of juice outside. Check the rim of anything either child drinks from before it reaches a mouth. Neither of them has been stung before, so watch for swelling round the face or mouth and know where the antihistamine is kept.

days.title: Ten Things in the Rucksack
days.prepTonight: Heap twenty things she might pack on the floor by the rucksack, and check the finds box from Friday is where she left it.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: What Goes In and What Stays Home

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Book With Nothing Made Up In It

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Library Books on the Floor

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Garden Book, Read Back to Her

opening.title: What Goes In and What Stays Home
opening.need: 1 rucksack or tote bag · about 20 things she might pack, heaped on the floor · 1 sheet of paper · 1 crayon.
steps: Sit on the floor with the heap between you. She holds each thing up and says take it or leave it. The leavers go back in the pile behind you.
Ten go in the bag. The moment she has eleven, one has to come out, and she chooses which.
Draw the ten on the paper as she packs, so she can check the bag against the list without unpacking it.

main.title: One Thing At Every Stop
materials: 10 packable items: 1 apple, a handful of crackers, 1 cup, 1 small bottle of water, 1 stick of chalk, 1 length of string, 1 cloth, 1 bandage, 1 spoon, 1 small toy
1 second stick of chalk, for marking the stops
steps: Name the ten stops before you go out the door: back step, gate, fence corner, trash can, front door, lamp post, mailbox, low wall, bench, home.

One thing comes out at each stop and gets used there. The crackers get eaten at the gate. Her chalk draws at the fence corner. The string ties something to the gate post. The cloth wipes the bench. The spoon digs the border. The cup and bottle make a drink stop on the low wall. The bandage goes on a knee that does not need it. The apple and the toy stay for the last two.
Count what is left out loud after every stop. Nine, eight, seven. Let her say the number before you do.
Anything worth keeping goes into the finds box on her shoulder, so it fills while the bag empties.
Mark each stop with a cross using your second stick of chalk, one cross for any pair you ran together. She can walk the route backwards tomorrow and count up.
At the last stop, hand her the empty bag and let her turn it upside down and shake it.
main.tip: Ten stops in an hour is one every six minutes, and she will want to stay at the third. Let her, and run stops seven and eight together at the low wall, so the bag still empties by the last stop.

outside.title: Where the Spiders Built Overnight
paras: This is the best week of the year for webs. Go out early to the fences, the hedge tops and the gaps between the trash cans, and look for the round ones strung overnight. Breathe on one and watch it shake. Count how many you find on one fence run. Nothing gets touched, because a broken web costs the spider its whole night.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and points at pictures in books, the same finger he uses out here. Hold him up level with a web and wait. When he points, name it and say something about it rather than repeating the word.

second.title: The Book With Nothing Made Up In It
second.intro: Three sheets of paper, stapled once, and every page has to be something that exists. The finds table is the whole source list.
materials: The week's finds, on the table by the window
steps: Stack the three sheets, fold them in half together and staple or tape the fold. Five pages and a cover.
She walks to the finds table and picks five things, one for each page. Only five, so something she likes gets left out.
One thing per page, drawn by her. No dragons and no invented animals.
Ask her what each page should say and write her exact words underneath with the marker. Keep the bits that are not sentences.
She does the cover: her name, and a title she chooses out loud before you write it.
Read it back to her once, all the way through, in the voice you would use for a printed book.
It goes in her bag at half past two and comes to the library with her.
second.tip: Five pages is the entire book. A ten-page one gets abandoned at page four.

alternatives: One page, one find, one sentence, and read it four times.
Make the book about Kreston instead, one page per thing he did today.
Photograph the five finds and stick the prints in instead of drawing.
Skip the book and sort the whole finds table into what came from a plant and what did not.
outAgain: The library, the every two weeks one, and her book goes with her
Indoor playground, if the library has a storytime session filling the place
The park on the walk back, for twenty minutes on the way home
The bench outside the library, to read the new books before you get home
The bookstore window, if the library is shut for the afternoon
days.krestonPM: The board book corner is his whole visit. At 15 months he points at pictures and waits for you to name them, and he will point at the same dog eleven times. Let Azlyn choose one book for him and carry it to the desk herself. Twenty minutes is about his limit.

insight.headline: Subtraction makes sense long before the symbols do.
paras: Azlyn can track a bag going from six things to five without any idea what a minus sign is. Three-year-olds handle take-away problems with real objects years ahead of handling them on paper, and the requirement is that the quantity is visible and the change is something she did with her own hands. Counting down out loud as the bag empties gives her the number line running the direction school will later call harder. When she meets it written down at six, the sum will be a new notation for something her hands sorted out on a Wednesday in September.

days.safety: Three of the ten stops sit on the curb. Kreston rides the lamp post, the mailbox and the bench in the stroller or on your hip, and the brake goes on before the rucksack comes off your shoulder. Azlyn kneels and unpacks on the house side of the sidewalk with you between her and the traffic, and she stops at every driveway line and looks before she crosses it. The stapler is adult only. You press it, she holds the fold, and it goes back in the drawer between books. Leave every web where it is, because a broken one costs the spider its whole night, and nothing off a fence, a wall or a trash can lid goes near either of their mouths.

days.title: Two Pairs of Hands
days.prepTonight: Carry the broom handle, the big towel and the old sheet out to the back door, empty the three pots, and stand the unopened bag of potting soil outside by the step.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Pot With Nothing In It Yet

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Nail Brush and a Long Bath

opening.title: The Sheet That Takes Two
opening.need: 1 old sheet · the clothesline and pegs.
steps: Two corners each, and pull until the sheet is tight between you. Let go of one and let her feel the whole thing drop.
Clip it on the line together. She holds the weight while you peg one corner, then she pegs the low end.
Take it down and fold it: corners to corners, walk your two across to hers, hand them over. Tell her every job at quarter past nine needs two.

main.title: The Two-Person Carry
materials: 1 heavy pot, or a bag of soil
steps: Slide the broom handle through the bucket handle. One end on your shoulder, one in both her hands, and walk the yard in step. You stop when she says stop.
Half the water will be on the path by the far end. Fill it and walk it back slower.
Lay the heavy pot in the middle of the towel. Two corners each, lift on three, and carry it where she says.
Spread the old sheet flat on the grass, a corner each, then fold it the way you did at eight.
Clip the wet towel on the line. She hands you pegs for the high end and does the low end.
Try the bucket with one person. Let her heave at it alone before you pick up the other end.
main.tip: Walking in step is the hard part. Count out loud, left and left and left, and let her take over the count.

outside.title: Pulling Up What's Finished
paras: The beans are done and the tomato stalks have gone hard and yellow. Go round the borders pulling up everything that has finished, one of you on the stem and one on the base, both leaning back. Some come out on the first pull and some take four. Shake the soil off the roots onto the bed, and let her decide which plants are finished.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and carries things while he runs, so give him the empty bucket and a short route to take it along. He mouths whatever he carries, so the pulled plants stay out of his hands and he keeps the bucket the whole time.

second.title: The Pot With Nothing In It Yet
second.intro: Three pots get filled, watered and labeled with nothing. What goes in them has not been chosen yet.
materials: 3 plant pots, or large tins and yogurt tubs with holes punched in the bottom
1 bag of potting soil, or garden soil
1 trowel, or a big serving spoon
A handful of stones or gravel
3 craft sticks and 1 permanent marker for the labels
steps: Spread the old sheet and stand the three pots on it.
Open the bag of potting soil at arm's length, turned away from both of them, and let the first cloud of dust blow off.
A layer of stones in the bottom of each pot so the water has somewhere to go. She counts them in.
She fills each pot with the trowel, three-quarters up, pressed down flat with her palm.
Water all three from the pitcher so the soil settles and drops. Top them up to the same level.
Push a craft stick into each pot and leave the marker beside them. The labels stay blank until tonight.
Say out loud what happens next: garden center at half past two, she chooses three, and they go in at four o'clock.
second.tip: Give her the number in the parking lot rather than in the aisle. Three plants and nothing else.

alternatives: Fill one pot instead of three, by hand, no trowel.
Plant seeds from the packet drawer and skip the garden center.
Move the three empty pots round the yard and work out which spot gets the sun.
Line the pots up on the finds table and draw what she thinks will come up.
outAgain: The garden center, three plants, chosen by her, and she carries the small one
The hardware store, if the garden center is a drive too far today
A neighbor's garden, to ask for a cutting instead of buying
The park, with the pots left waiting on the step
The supermarket plant rack, a quarter of the price
days.krestonPM: At 15 months he points at everything in a garden center and wants to touch it. Give him a cart to push or a small pot to carry. Keep him out of the aisles with the bagged feed and the slug pellets.

insight.headline: Cooperation is harder than competition, and it needs the same practice.
paras: Racing needs one thing from Azlyn: her own goal. Working with you needs four. She has to hold a shared goal, take a role inside it, watch what your end of the bucket is doing, and adjust to it in real time. Researchers who set up tasks that cannot be done alone find three-year-olds managing more of it than they manage when the same job could be done by one person. Nothing you say about teamwork does what a broom handle with two people on it does. Every job in this yard today is built so that letting go has a visible consequence.

days.safety: Bagged potting soil throws up dust and bacteria when it is first opened, so open it at arm's length, outside, and away from both their faces. Kreston is 15 months and will eat a fistful of soil given three seconds alone with it, so the open bag stays up on the step and he works at the far end of the sheet. Stay within arm's reach of him for every minute the bucket holds water, and tip it out on the grass the moment the carrying stops. Hands and nails scrubbed before any food, which is what the nail brush is for at five. Tomato stalks and leaves poison a child who chews them, so every plant you pull goes straight on a pile at the far end of the bed, out of his reach, and nothing green goes in his hands. Check whatever comes home from the garden center for berries before it goes anywhere he can reach.
